## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0550-virtual-environments-python-uv-quarto.qmd >}}

## Why this needs its own chapter

A Quarto document with Python chunks runs that Python somewhere.
In a uv project you want it to run in the project's `.venv`,
with the packages `uv.lock` records.
`quarto render` on its own does not know about your project.
`uv run quarto render` does.

This chapter shows the difference with a small project,
`quarto-demo`,
and one document, `report.qmd`,
that prints which Python ran it and which pandas it found:

````{.markdown filename="report.qmd"}
---
title: "Which Python?"
format: html
---

```{{python}}
import sys
import pandas as pd

print(sys.executable)
print(pd.__version__)
```
````

## What Quarto needs from your project

Quarto runs Python chunks through Jupyter,
so the project's environment needs a few packages besides the ones your analysis uses:

- `ipykernel`, the kernel that runs the Python code
- `nbclient`, which Quarto uses to run the chunks one after another
- `pyyaml`, which Quarto's own Jupyter runner imports

The [docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv) example project
(MIT licence) lists exactly these, with the comment "Quarto needs these to run Python code".
Here is the demo project's `pyproject.toml`
after `uv add pandas ipykernel nbclient pyyaml`,
with exact pins as in [uv: pinning exact versions](0545-virtual-environments-python-uv-exact-pins.qmd):

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[project]
name = "quarto-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "ipykernel==7.4.0",
    "nbclient==0.11.0",
    "pandas==3.1.1",
    "pyyaml==6.0.3",
]

[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"
```

## How Quarto picks a Python

If the `QUARTO_PYTHON` environment variable is set,
Quarto uses the Python it names.
Otherwise, on macOS and Linux,
Quarto uses the first `python3` on your `PATH`.
On Windows, it asks the Python launcher, `py`, which Python to use.

`quarto check jupyter` tells you which Python that is.
Here it is in a new terminal on a Mac,
inside the `quarto-demo` folder:

```bash
quarto check jupyter
```

```out
Quarto 1.11.6
[✓] Checking Python 3 installation....OK
      Version: 3.15.2
      Path: /opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.15/bin/python3.15
      Jupyter: (None)

      Jupyter is not available in this Python installation.
      Install with python3 -m pip install jupyter

      There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv. Did you forget to activate it?
```

Quarto found Homebrew's Python 3.15,
the first `python3` on the `PATH`.
The project pins 3.14,
and the packages are in `.venv`, not in Homebrew's Python.

Quarto even notices the `.venv` folder
and suggests activating it.
You do not need to.
Do not follow the other suggestion either.
Installing Jupyter into Homebrew's Python with `pip`
puts packages outside your project,
where `uv.lock` does not record them.

## What `uv run` changes

For the one command it runs,
`uv run` puts the project's `.venv/bin` folder first on the `PATH`
and sets the `VIRTUAL_ENV` environment variable to the project's `.venv`.
On macOS and Linux, the first `python3` Quarto finds is then the project's.
On Windows, the Python launcher runs the Python of the environment named in `VIRTUAL_ENV`,
which is the same one:

```bash
uv run quarto check jupyter
```

```out
Quarto 1.11.6
[✓] Checking Python 3 installation....OK
      Version: 3.14.3
      Path: /Users/dan/quarto-demo/.venv/bin/python3
      Jupyter: 5.9.1
      Kernels: python3

[✓] Checking Jupyter engine render....OK
```

Same folder, same Quarto,
a different Python.
The path now ends in `quarto-demo/.venv/bin/python3`,
the version is the pinned 3.14,
and Jupyter is there because `ipykernel` and `nbclient` are in the project.

:::{.callout-note title="On Windows"}
The `Path:` line should end in `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`.
If it does not,
for example because your Python came from `uv` and the Python launcher `py` is not installed,
set `QUARTO_PYTHON` as shown in the last section of this chapter.
:::

## Rendering, without and with `uv run`

Without `uv run`, the render fails:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd
```

```out
Starting python3 kernel...Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../share/jupyter/jupyter.py", line 20, in <module>
    from notebook import notebook_execute, RestartKernel
  File ".../share/jupyter/notebook.py", line 15, in <module>
    from yaml import safe_load as parse_string
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'
Python 3 installation:
{}
Jupyter is not available in this Python installation.
Install with python3 -m pip install jupyter
There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv. Did you forget to activate it?
WARN: Error encountered when rendering files
```

The `ModuleNotFoundError` is about Quarto's own runner,
which needs `pyyaml`,
not about your code.
It fails before your first chunk runs.

With `uv run`, it works:

```bash
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

```out
Output created: report.html
```

and the report shows the project's Python and the locked pandas:

```out
/Users/dan/quarto-demo/.venv/bin/python3
3.1.1
```

For a Quarto project with a `_quarto.yml`,
such as a website or a book,
it is the same, `uv run quarto render` from the project folder.
`quarto preview` becomes `uv run quarto preview`.

## The failure you do not see

A failed render is the good case,
because you know something is wrong.
The bad case is a render that works with the wrong Python.

Suppose your terminal still has another project's environment activated,
one that happens to have Jupyter and an older pandas.
Plain `quarto render` finds that environment's Python first on the `PATH`,
and succeeds:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd
```

```out
Output created: report.html
```

```out
/Users/dan/other-project/.venv/bin/python3
3.0.5
```

The report rendered with pandas 3.0.5,
not the 3.1.1 that this project's `uv.lock` records,
and nothing warned you.
If the two versions compute something differently,
your report shows numbers your collaborators cannot reproduce.

`uv run` ignores the other environment,
tells you so,
and uses the project's:

```bash
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

```out
warning: `VIRTUAL_ENV=/Users/dan/other-project/.venv` does not match the project environment path `.venv` and will be ignored; use `--active` to target the active environment instead
Output created: report.html
```

```out
/Users/dan/quarto-demo/.venv/bin/python3
3.1.1
```

To check which Python a render will use,
run `quarto check jupyter` the same way you render,
with `uv run` in front,
and read the `Path:` line.

## Without `uv run`, use `QUARTO_PYTHON`

If a tool runs `quarto render` for you and you cannot add `uv run` in front,
point `QUARTO_PYTHON` at the project's Python instead:

::: {.panel-tabset group="shell"}
## macOS and Linux

```bash
QUARTO_PYTHON=.venv/bin/python quarto render report.qmd
```

## Windows (Git Bash)

```bash
QUARTO_PYTHON=.venv/Scripts/python.exe quarto render report.qmd
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
$env:QUARTO_PYTHON = ".venv\Scripts\python.exe"
quarto render report.qmd
```
:::

On macOS:

```out
Output created: report.html
```

```out
/Users/dan/quarto-demo/.venv/bin/python
3.1.1
```

`QUARTO_PYTHON` has two costs compared with `uv run`.
You have to set it again on every render
(or once per session in PowerShell),
and it does not check that `.venv` matches `uv.lock`,
which `uv run` does before every command.
Prefer `uv run`.

## Put it in the Makefile

The easiest way to never forget `uv run` is to not type the command at all.
A Makefile target writes it down once:

```make
render: ## Render the report with the project's Python
	uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

This book does the same.
Its own `Makefile` renders and previews the book with
`uv run quarto render book/` and `uv run quarto preview`,
so `make render` always uses the book's `.venv`.
